label: Integral Curves and Flows
notes: This chapter, printed pages 205 through 248, is an ODE laboratory written in manifold language. A single smooth vector field controls a whole family of geometric objects: its integral curves, its maximal flow, the coordinates it straightens, and the characteristic curves that solve first-order partial differential equations. We follow that chain end to end.

label: Integral Curves
notes: Start from the defining equation rather than any picture. An integral curve is a curve whose velocity at every instant equals the field evaluated at the point it currently occupies. In a chart this is a first-order autonomous ordinary differential equation, so the geometric notion becomes the analytic one we already know how to solve locally.

label: Existence and Uniqueness
notes: The fundamental existence and uniqueness theorem for ordinary differential equations does all the analytic heavy lifting. Smoothness of the field gives a unique integral curve through each starting point on some open time interval, and curves sharing initial data agree where both are defined. Solutions also depend smoothly on the initial point, which we will need immediately for flows.

label: Flows
notes: Solving every initial value problem at once assembles the integral curves into a single map theta. Fixing the point traces its curve; fixing the time gives a diffeomorphism that slides the whole manifold along the curves. The group law theta_t after theta_s equals theta_{t+s} makes this a one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms, the algebraic heart of the chapter.

label: The Fundamental Theorem on Flows
notes: Every smooth vector field generates exactly one maximal flow. Its domain is an open subset of the real line times the manifold containing the zero slice, each time slice is open, and on it theta_t is a diffeomorphism onto another slice with inverse theta_{-t}. The vector field is recovered as the infinitesimal generator, the t-derivative of the flow at time zero.

label: Flow Domains and Maximality
notes: A local solution is not a global action; the domain is part of the object. The field x squared d-dx on the line blows up in finite time, while plain translation on the punctured plane escapes by running into the missing origin. Maximality records these genuine obstructions: blow-up, missing points, and escape from every compact set.

label: Complete Vector Fields
notes: A vector field is complete when its flow is defined for all real time, giving a genuine one-parameter group acting on the whole manifold. Compactly supported fields are complete, and as a corollary so is every smooth field on a compact manifold, since a curve leaving every compact set is the only way maximal time can stay finite.

label: Flowout and Canonical Form
notes: Flow a hypersurface that the field never touches tangentially, and the flowout map sending pair t and s to theta_t of the point becomes a local diffeomorphism near the surface. In the resulting coordinates the vector field is simply the coordinate field d-dt. This canonical-form theorem says any nonvanishing field looks locally like straight, parallel, unit-speed flow lines.

label: The Lie Derivative
notes: Comparing one vector field to another is subtle because nearby field values live in different tangent spaces. The flow of V supplies the missing identification: pull W back along the inverse flow into one tangent space, then differentiate at time zero. That derivative is the Lie derivative of W with respect to V, the infinitesimal change of W as the flow drags it.

label: Lie Derivative Equals the Bracket
notes: The central computation identifies the Lie derivative with the Lie bracket: L_V W equals bracket V W. For V the x-translation and W equal to x times d-dy, pulling back changes the field by t times d-dy, so the derivative is d-dy, exactly the bracket. This turns an analytic limit into pure commutator algebra of differential operators.

label: Commuting Flows
notes: Two fields commute as operators exactly when their flows commute as maps. Move time t along one then time s along the other; if the bracket vanishes the two routes close on the same point, and the fields can be completed to a coordinate grid. When the bracket is nonzero the flow square opens by a second-order gap measured precisely by that bracket.

label: Time-Dependent Fields
notes: Allowing the field to depend on time forces the flow to carry two time arguments, the current time and the starting time, not merely elapsed time. The model x over t on positive t has flow t over t-naught times x-naught. Composition uses the middle time through a cocycle law rather than simple addition of times.

label: First-Order PDE Characteristics
notes: The flowout viewpoint becomes the method of characteristics. A first-order Cauchy problem reduces to ordinary differential equations along characteristic curves traced by an associated field. For the quasilinear case the unknown becomes a coordinate and the solution graph is built as a flowout in one higher dimension. Noncharacteristic initial data is the transversality that makes a local graph solution exist.

label: Recap
notes: We turned one smooth vector field into integral curves, a unique maximal flow, completeness criteria, straightening coordinates, the Lie derivative equal to the bracket, a commuting-flows test, time-dependent cocycles, and the method of characteristics. The recurring idea is that flowing along a field converts geometry and partial differential equations into ordinary differential equations we can solve.
